questions.text: The wiring: a relay built from two kinds of cell

steps.bridge: A slow door and fast cables. The reason is that they are made of two different kinds of cell.

lesson.text:
Start with the heart's problem. Billions of muscle cells must squeeze in a fixed order: atria first, then a pause, then both ventricles together. No nerve tells each cell when to go. The heart does it with a relay, each cell passing the signal to the next. Follow one beat down it, because every block you'll meet later is a fault at a named point on this road.

The beat is born in the SA node, a small strip of cells high in the right atrium, where the superior vena cava enters. From there the signal spreads across the atrial muscle like a ripple across a pond. A band of fibres called the Bachmann bundle carries it quickly to the left atrium, and the internodal pathways carry it down to the floor of the right atrium.

Now the ripple meets a wall. Between the atria and the ventricles lies a ring of fibrous tissue that doesn't conduct electricity at all. [[There is exactly one electrical door through that ring, and it is the AV node, low in the wall between the two atria.]] Here the signal slows to a crawl, on purpose, for about a tenth of a second. Why would a heart want a delay? It gives the atria time to finish squeezing, so the last top-up of blood, the atrial kick, reaches the ventricles before they contract. And the door is a guard. If the atria ever race at three or four hundred a minute, the slow door lets only some of those signals through.

Past the door, everything is built for speed. The bundle of His pierces the fibrous ring and runs into the septum between the ventricles. There it splits into a right bundle branch and a left bundle branch. The left one divides again into a thin anterior fascicle and a broad posterior fascicle. So picture three cables below the His bundle. They end in the Purkinje fibres, a fine net under the inner lining of both ventricles. The net delivers the signal to the whole inner surface almost at once, and the muscle passes it outwards, from the inner lining, the endocardium, to the outer surface, the epicardium.

One detail matters later. The first piece of ventricle to fire is the septum, and it fires from its left side to its right, because the left bundle gives off its first twigs there. Septum first, left to right: in the camera section that explains the small r wave in V1.

Now the speeds. The AV node is slowest, at about zero point zero five metres a second. The Purkinje fibres are fastest, at two to four metres a second. Ordinary muscle sits in between, at about a third of a metre to one metre a second. Guyton gives zero point three to zero point five, and Ganong gives one.

Next, the back-up system. Every level of the relay can make its own beat, but each lower level is slower. The SA node fires at sixty to one hundred a minute, the AV junction at forty to sixty, and the ventricles at only twenty to forty. Normally the lower ones are silent, because each beat from above resets them before they can fire. That is overdrive suppression: the fastest pacemaker wins. When the top fails, or the door is blocked, the next one down takes over, and its rate tells you where it lives. That's an escape rhythm.

{{**The relay:** SA node → atria → **AV node (slow door)** → His → right bundle + left bundle (anterior and posterior fascicles) → Purkinje → muscle, endocardium to epicardium
**Back-up rates:** SA 60–100 | AV junction 40–60 | ventricle 20–40
**Speeds:** AV node ≈ 0.05 m/s | muscle ≈ 0.3–1 m/s (Guyton 0.3–0.5; Ganong 1) | Purkinje 2–4 m/s}}

Last, the blood supply, because it predicts which infarct breaks which part. The SA node's artery comes off the right coronary in about sixty per cent of people and off the circumflex in about forty. The AV node's artery comes off the right coronary in about ninety per cent. So an inferior infarct starves the node itself. The cables below run in the septum, fed mainly by the left anterior descending, so an anterior infarct damages the wiring below the node. NEET likes to offer the left anterior descending as the AV node's artery.

[[SA node sixty to one hundred, AV junction forty to sixty, ventricle twenty to forty: the fastest pacemaker wins. The AV node's artery comes from the right coronary in about nine people in ten.]]

So the relay has a slow door in the middle and fast cables beyond it. Why is one part slow and the other fast? Because they are built from two different kinds of cell.
lesson.cap: The relay: SA node → atria → AV node (the delay gate) → His → bundles → Purkinje. Back-up rates fall with each level: 60–100, 40–60, 20–40.

steps.bridge: The nerves speak to the calcium cells. Next: how vagus and sympathetic act, and where atropine can and cannot work.

lesson.text:
Here is the idea that the whole of the ECG stands on. The heart's electrical system is built from two kinds of cell, and they differ in one thing: which ion fires them.

Every heart cell fires by opening gates in its wall and letting positive ions rush in. That inward rush is the upstroke. In most of the heart the gates are sodium gates. In the two nodes they are calcium gates.

Take the sodium cell first. Atrial muscle, the His bundle, the bundle branches, the Purkinje fibres and ventricular muscle: everything except the two nodes. At rest a sodium cell sits at a steady minus ninety millivolts. When the signal arrives, thousands of sodium gates slam open together and the voltage leaps up within a millisecond or two. A steep, tall upstroke is a strong shove to the next cell, so the signal travels fast. And it is all or none. A sodium cell either fires fully and passes the signal on at full speed, or it fails completely. There is no half measure, and no warning. Picture a light switch. It works every time, until the day it doesn't.

Now the calcium cell: the SA node and the AV node. It has almost no working sodium gates. Its upstroke is carried by L-type calcium gates, which open slowly and carry a smaller current. So the upstroke is a gentle slope, the shove to the next cell is weak, and the signal creeps. That is why the AV node is the slow door. It also has no steady resting level: its voltage drifts upwards between beats, which the next section uses to explain the pacemaker.

The calcium cell has one more property, and it's the important one. After it fires, it needs time to recover, and that recovery runs on a clock. A sodium cell is ready again almost as soon as its voltage has come back down. A calcium cell stays sluggish for a while after its voltage has fully recovered. So if the next signal arrives a little early, the node is only partly recovered, and it conducts that signal more slowly. Drive it faster and it conducts more slowly still, until one signal fails to get through. Then the node gets a full rest and the cycle starts again. This is called decremental conduction. Picture a worker who needs a breather between jobs. Hand him the jobs too close together and each one takes a little longer, until he misses one, catches his breath, and starts fresh.

You have just heard the two kinds of heart block, before we've named them. A tired node that takes longer and longer and then drops a beat is a calcium cell. A cable below the node that drops a beat suddenly, with no lengthening before it, is a sodium cell: all or none. The second ECG packet builds Mobitz one and Mobitz two on exactly that.

[[The node is calcium and the wiring below it is sodium. Calcium cells conduct slowly and tire gradually, so they fail with a warning. Sodium cells conduct fast and all or none, so they fail without one.]]

The same split tells you what acts where. The calcium cells are the ones the nerves and the node drugs speak to. The vagus slows them. So does adenosine. So do beta-blockers, verapamil and diltiazem. So does digoxin, which acts on the node largely through the vagus. All of them slow the sinus rate or slow the door, and at ordinary doses none of them widens the QRS complex. The sodium cells answer to different things: the sodium channel blockers, such as flecainide, lidocaine and an overdose of tricyclic antidepressants; a high potassium; and ischaemia. These slow conduction through the cables and the muscle, and they widen the QRS.

{{**Calcium cells (SA node, AV node)** | **Sodium cells (atria, His, bundles, Purkinje, ventricle)**
Slow, decremental, fail gradually | Fast, all or none, fail suddenly
Vagus, adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin | Sodium-channel blockers, high K⁺, ischaemia
Slow rate, long PR | Wide QRS}}

NEET's favourite confusion treats all conduction as one tissue: lidocaine offered to slow the AV node, or a wide QRS offered for verapamil. Ask one question. Is this a calcium cell or a sodium cell?

We've now said twice that the nerves act on the nodes, without saying how. How does the vagus slow a node, and why does atropine work in some slow hearts and fail in others?
lesson.cap: Two kinds of cell. Node = calcium: slow, tires gradually. Below the node = sodium: fast, all-or-none.

steps.bridge: Both nerves work on the drift between beats. Next section: that drift, phase four, and the other phases that draw the waves.

lesson.text:
Two sets of nerves have their hands on the relay, and both hold it mainly at the calcium cells. That tells you where atropine works, where it can't, and why a strain and a drug stop the same tachycardia.

Start with the vagus, the brake. Its endings release acetylcholine onto a receptor called M2, on the cells of the SA node and the AV node. M2 does two things. It opens potassium channels, so positive charge leaks out and the cell is pulled more negative, further from firing. And it lowers the cell's cyclic AMP, which makes the upward drift between beats shallower. The SA node slows, and the AV node conducts more slowly. The geography matters more than the chemistry. Vagal fibres are dense around the two nodes and the atria, and sparse in the His bundle, the bundle branches and the ventricles. The vagus has almost no grip below the node.

The sympathetic nerves are the accelerator. Noradrenaline and adrenaline act on the beta one receptor, which is coupled to a G protein called Gs. Gs switches on the enzyme adenylate cyclase, which makes cyclic AMP. Cyclic AMP steepens the drift in the SA node, so the rate rises, and it opens more calcium gates, so the AV node conducts faster and the muscle contracts harder. A grand test asked you for the second messenger of adrenaline's beta effect. It is cyclic AMP, made by adenylate cyclase. The tempting wrong option was phospholipase C, which belongs to the alpha one receptor, through Gq, in the blood vessels.

[[Beta receptors work through Gs, adenylate cyclase and cyclic AMP. Phospholipase C belongs to alpha one and Gq.]]

At rest the brake wins. A heart with no nerves beats at about one hundred a minute, so a resting seventy is the vagus holding it down.

Now atropine. It blocks the M2 receptor: it takes the foot off the brake, and that is all it does. So it works where the slowness is vagal and in a node: sinus bradycardia, and a block inside the AV node. It can't help a block below the node, because there was no vagal brake there to remove. And it fails in a transplanted heart, because the nerves were cut at the operation. Those patients need pacing or a direct beta stimulant, and the Arrest packet gives you the order.

[[Atropine only removes vagal tone, so it speeds the sinus node and the AV node. It does nothing for a block below the node, and nothing for a denervated transplanted heart.]]

Turn the same lever the other way. If a tachycardia is a circuit running through the AV node, shutting the door for a few seconds breaks it. A vagal manoeuvre does it through the patient's own reflex: the baroreceptors fire, the brainstem answers down the vagus, and the node stalls. Adenosine does it chemically. Its receptor on the nodal cell opens the very same potassium channels as acetylcholine. So adenosine is a vagal manoeuvre in a syringe, which is why the two sit side by side in the algorithm.

A grand test asked the manoeuvres as statements, and you lost that mark. Here are the true versions. The Valsalva is a sustained strain against a closed airway, not a deep breath in. The modified Valsalva is a strain at forty millimetres of mercury for fifteen seconds, semi-recumbent, then the patient is laid flat at once with the legs raised, so the rush of returning blood enlarges the reflex. In the REVERT trial it restored sinus rhythm in forty-three per cent, against seventeen per cent with the standard strain. Carotid sinus massage is done lying down, on a monitor, on one side only, for five to ten seconds, and never when there's a carotid bruit or a previous stroke or TIA. And because all of these act on the node, they end rhythms that use the node, only slow the ventricles briefly in atrial flutter or fibrillation, and don't stop ventricular tachycardia.

Adenosine's doses and fine print come in the Rhythm packet. What you need now is the picture underneath both nerves: that upward drift between beats.

spine: One beat runs SA node, atria, AV node, His bundle, three cables (right bundle, left anterior and posterior fascicles), Purkinje net, then muscle from inside out.
The AV node is the only door through the fibrous ring and is slow on purpose: it lets the atrial kick finish and shields the ventricles from fast atria.
Back-up pacemakers get slower going down: SA 60–100, AV junction 40–60, ventricle 20–40. The fastest wins (overdrive suppression).
Two kinds of cell: the nodes fire on calcium (slow, decremental, fail gradually); everything else fires on sodium (fast, all or none, fails suddenly).
Vagus (M2, potassium channels, less cAMP) and sympathetic (beta-1, Gs, adenylate cyclase, cAMP) both act mainly on the nodes.
So atropine, vagal manoeuvres and adenosine work at the node, and not on a block below it or (atropine) on a transplanted heart.

open.text:
Shock Two ended on a promise. Before the shock, there's the infarct. And the first thing you'll ever see of an infarct is a line on paper. So before the infarct, one step further back: the paper itself.

You've read ECG before, in bits and pieces. Most of us have. And when the bottom layer goes, everything built on top of it starts to look frightening. Mobitz one and Mobitz two. The R wave that should be small in V1. A long QT. Four classes of antiarrhythmic drug. Each one feels like a separate thing to memorise.

They aren't separate. [[Every wave on the ECG is one moment in the life of a heart cell, seen by a camera from one side of the chest.]] Learn the cell, learn the cameras, and most ECG questions become questions you can work out instead of remember.

So this packet builds from the ground. First, the wiring: the relay that carries each beat from the top of the heart to the bottom, and the two very different kinds of cell it's built from. That one difference, a slow calcium cell against a fast sodium cell, is going to explain every heart block in the next packet. Then the two action potentials, phase by phase, and the wave each phase draws. Then the twelve leads as twelve cameras, with one rule that gives you the axis, the R wave across the chest, and hypertrophy. And last, the cameras turned on ischaemia. Why an injured wall lifts the ST segment, which leads watch which artery, the infarcts the standard leads hide, and the changes that look like an infarct but aren't.

Listen for one idea that keeps coming back. Sodium, calcium, potassium. Each phase of the cell belongs to one ion, and every drug and every electrolyte that changes the ECG is pressing on one of them.

Start at the top of the heart, with the cell that fires first.

questions.text: Two action potentials become the waves

open.text:
The P wave and the QRS complex are the same event. Each is a sheet of sodium cells firing, one sheet in the atria and one in the ventricles, and each is drawn by the same phase of the same action potential. See that, and the ECG stops being shapes to memorise. It becomes the life of a cell, written out sideways.

You've met the two kinds of cell. Now we open each one up. A cell's voltage over one beat is its action potential, and its parts are numbered as phases. In the calcium cell the part that matters is the slow drift between beats, because that drift sets the heart rate. The sodium cell has five phases, and each draws one piece of the ECG.

Then the pay-off. If each phase is one current, anything that disturbs a current changes a predictable piece of the trace. That map carries you through electrolytes, poisons and the antiarrhythmic classes.

Listen for one trap. The ECG doesn't show voltage. It shows current flowing between cells that disagree. That is why the line can be flat while a great deal is happening.

Begin with the cell that starts every beat.

steps.bridge: The node keeps time and draws nothing. Next: the muscle cell, whose five phases draw the QRS, the ST segment and the T wave.

lesson.text:
You know the SA node fires on its own, sixty to a hundred times a minute. The question is how a cell that nobody commands keeps time.

Picture a cistern that fills from a tap and empties itself every time the water reaches a line. Nobody operates it. Its rhythm depends on three things only: how fast the tap runs, how high the line is, and how empty the cistern is when it starts. The SA node cell is that cistern, and its voltage is the water level.

Follow one cycle. Just after a beat the cell is at its most negative, about minus sixty millivolts. That lowest point is called the maximum diastolic potential. A muscle cell would sit still there. The node cell can't, because of the HCN channel, which carries the funny current. It's funny because it behaves backwards. Almost every other channel in the heart opens when the cell becomes more positive. This one opens when the cell becomes negative. So the moment the cell reaches its lowest voltage, the funny channel opens, sodium trickles in, and the voltage begins to climb. [[That slow climb is phase four, the pacemaker potential, and its steepness sets the heart rate.]] Near the top of the climb a short-lived calcium channel, the T type, helps with the last few millivolts.

At about minus forty millivolts the cell reaches threshold. Now the L-type calcium gates open and the cell fires. This is phase zero, and remember it's a calcium upstroke, so it's a slope and not a spike. Then potassium channels open, positive charge leaves, and the voltage falls back towards minus sixty. That's phase three. And as it gets there, the funny channel opens again. The cycle restarts itself.

Notice which numbers are missing. The node cell has no phase one and no phase two. Those belong to the sodium cell, in the next step.

So there are three ways to change the rate, the three things about the cistern. The slope of the climb: the tap. The starting level, the maximum diastolic potential: start lower and the climb takes longer. And the threshold, the line: raise it and the climb takes longer.

Put the nerves from the last step onto this picture. The sympathetic nerves raise cyclic AMP, and cyclic AMP binds directly to the funny channel and opens it more readily. The tap runs faster, the slope steepens, the rate rises. Fever and an overactive thyroid steepen it too. The vagus does two things at once. It lowers cyclic AMP, which turns the tap down, and it opens potassium channels, which starts the cistern from a lower level. Adenosine uses those same potassium channels. Beta-blockers turn the tap down by blocking the sympathetic drive. Verapamil and diltiazem block the L-type calcium gates and weaken the upstroke, which shows most at the AV node. Cold and an underactive thyroid flatten the slope.

One drug acts on the funny channel and nothing else: ivabradine. It turns the tap down and touches no other current. So the sinus rate falls, with no change in contractility and no fall in blood pressure. That's the fact NEET asks. And because it acts only on the sinus node's own pacemaker current, it does nothing for the rate in atrial fibrillation, where the sinus node isn't in charge.

{{**Nodal action potential:** phase 4 = If (HCN, "funny"), then T-type Ca²⁺ → threshold ≈ −40 mV → phase 0 = L-type Ca²⁺ → phase 3 = K⁺ out → back to ≈ −60 mV. No phase 1 or 2.
**Rate changes by:** slope of phase 4 | threshold | maximum diastolic potential}}

Last, something that surprises people. When the SA node fires, the ECG shows nothing. The node is a tiny cluster of cells, far too small a current to move the pen. The first thing you see, the P wave, is the atrial muscle answering. You infer the sinus node from a P wave of the right shape before every QRS: upright in lead two and upside down in aVR. The camera section shows why.

[[Ivabradine blocks only the funny current, so it slows the sinus rate without changing contractility or blood pressure. The SA node's own firing is invisible on the ECG; the P wave is the atria answering.]]

So the calcium cell keeps time. Now the cell that does the work, and draws nearly everything on the paper.
lesson.cap: Phase 4 sets the rate. Flatter slope, a more negative starting point or a higher threshold = slower firing.

steps.bridge: Shapes need a ruler. Next: what one small square means, and the normal PR, QRS and QT.

lesson.text:
The ECG does not record voltage. It records current flowing between cells that are at different voltages. If every cell in the ventricle is at the same voltage, whatever that voltage is, the line is flat. Hold that, and the five phases of the muscle cell draw the ECG for you.

Phase four is rest. The cell sits at minus ninety millivolts, held there by a potassium channel that is open at rest and by the sodium potassium pump. There's no drift. This cell waits to be told.

Phase zero is the upstroke. The signal arrives, the sodium gates slam open, and the voltage leaps from minus ninety to about plus twenty in a millisecond or two. Then those gates snap shut and lock. Now think of the whole ventricle. For a moment some cells have fired and some haven't. They disagree, current flows between them, and that boundary sweeps through the muscle. The ECG draws the sweep as the QRS. In the atria the same phase zero draws the P wave.

Phase one is a small notch: a brief potassium current, the transient outward current, lets a little charge out. It is larger in the outer layer of the wall, the epicardium, and largest in the epicardium of the right ventricle. Park that. It is the seed of the J wave of hypothermia and of the Brugada pattern, both in the second packet.

Phase two is the plateau. Calcium flows in through L-type gates while potassium flows out, and the two balance, so the voltage hovers near zero for about a quarter of a second. The calcium coming in is the trigger for contraction. And on the ECG? Every ventricular cell is now on its plateau, at about the same voltage. No disagreement, no current, a flat line. That flat line is the ST segment, flat for the same reason as the baseline between beats: all the cells agree. An injured region that can't hold its plateau will disagree with its neighbours, and that is how ischaemia shifts the ST segment.

Phase three is repolarisation. The calcium gates close, and potassium currents carry positive charge out until the cell is back at minus ninety. The cells don't all finish together, so again there is disagreement, and the ECG draws the T wave. It is rounder than the QRS because each cell recovers in its own time, not along the fast wiring.

[[Phase zero, sodium in, draws the QRS. Phase two, calcium in balanced by potassium out, is the flat ST segment. Phase three, potassium out, draws the T wave. The QT interval, from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave, is the whole action potential.]]

{{**Phase 4** rest, −90 mV (IK1, Na⁺/K⁺ pump) | baseline
**Phase 0** Na⁺ in | **QRS** (P wave in atria)
**Phase 1** K⁺ out, brief (Ito) | J point
**Phase 2** Ca²⁺ in = K⁺ out | **ST segment**
**Phase 3** K⁺ out (IKr, IKs) | **T wave**
**Phase 0 to end of 3** | **QT**}}

Now a puzzle. Repolarisation is the electrical opposite of depolarisation, so why is the T wave upright where the QRS is upright? Because it also runs in the opposite direction. The epicardial cells fire last, but their action potentials are shorter, so they recover first. Depolarisation travels from the inside of the wall outwards; repolarisation travels from the outside inwards. An opposite charge moving in the opposite direction gives the same deflection. The atria repolarise too, but that small wave is buried under the QRS.

Next, the locked gates. From phase zero until about the middle of phase three the sodium gates are locked, and no stimulus can fire the cell: the absolute refractory period. In late phase three some gates have reset and some haven't, so a strong stimulus can fire the cell but the response spreads unevenly: the relative refractory period. On the ECG that is the T wave, and the dangerous moment is near its peak. A premature beat landing there, the R on T, can start ventricular fibrillation. That is why a cardioversion shock is synchronised to the R wave.

Last, the U wave: a small bump after the T wave, best seen in V2 and V3, thought to be late repolarisation of the Purkinje fibres. A big one means slow repolarisation, classically low potassium.

You now have the shapes. Before using them, you need the ruler.
lesson.cap: Each phase draws one wave: phase 0 (sodium) = QRS, phase 2 plateau (calcium) = flat ST, phase 3 (potassium) = T. The whole action potential = QT.

steps.bridge: Now disturb one current at a time, and watch which number on the paper changes.

lesson.text:
Everything so far has been a shape. The paper turns shapes into numbers, and it has only two scales.

Sideways is time. The paper runs at twenty-five millimetres a second. So one small square, one millimetre, is zero point zero four seconds, and one large square, five small ones, is zero point two seconds. Five large squares make one second. Upwards is voltage. Ten millimetres, two large squares, is one millivolt, and the rectangular calibration mark at the start of the strip proves the machine is set that way. Check it before you call anything big or small.

Rate comes straight from the time scale. Three hundred large squares pass in a minute. So count the large squares between two R waves and divide three hundred by that number. One square apart is three hundred a minute, two is one hundred and fifty, three is one hundred, four is seventy-five, five is sixty, six is fifty. For a finer answer, divide fifteen hundred by the number of small squares. Both methods assume a regular rhythm. When it's irregular, as in atrial fibrillation, they give a different answer for every pair of beats. Then count the QRS complexes on the full ten-second strip and multiply by six. NEET's trap is a single R to R interval offered on an irregular strip.

Now hang the normal numbers on the relay, because each interval is one stretch of that road.

The P wave is the atria firing. It lasts less than zero point one two seconds, which is three small squares, and it stands less than two and a half millimetres tall in lead two.

The PR interval runs from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS. It is the time from the atria firing to the ventricles firing, and most of it is the wait at the slow door, the AV node. Normal is zero point one two to zero point two zero seconds: three to five small squares. Longer than one large square means the door is slow. Shorter than three small squares means something got round the door.

The QRS is the ventricles firing. Because the Purkinje net delivers the signal everywhere almost at once, it's over in less than zero point one two seconds, and usually in zero point zero six to zero point one. That's why a narrow QRS tells you the beat came down the normal wiring. Between zero point one and zero point one two is a partial delay. Zero point one two or more is wide: the signal has had to cross muscle, cell to cell, the slow way.

The J point is the corner where the QRS ends and the ST segment begins. ST elevation and depression are measured there.

The QT interval, you'll recall, is the whole action potential. It shortens as the heart speeds up, so it is corrected for rate and written QTc. The upper limits to carry are about four hundred and fifty milliseconds in men and four hundred and sixty in women. A quick bedside check: at ordinary rates the QT should be less than half the R to R interval. The second packet shows you how to measure and correct it.

{{**Paper:** 25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV | small square 0.04 s | large square 0.2 s
**Rate:** 300 ÷ large squares, or 1500 ÷ small squares; irregular: QRS in 10 s × 6
**P** < 0.12 s, < 2.5 mm (lead II) | **PR** 0.12–0.20 s | **QRS** < 0.12 s (0.10–0.12 incomplete) | **QTc** ≤ 450 ms men, ≤ 460 ms women}}

[[One small square is zero point zero four seconds and one large square is zero point two. PR is three to five small squares. QRS is under three small squares. Rate is three hundred divided by the large squares between R waves.]]

With the ruler in your hand, go back to the phases and ask what happens to these numbers when one current is disturbed.
lesson.cap: 25 mm/s: small square 0.04 s, large square 0.2 s. PR 0.12–0.20 s, QRS < 0.12 s. ST is measured at the J point against the TP baseline.

steps.bridge: You know what each wave means. Next section: why the same wave is upright in one lead and inverted in another.

lesson.text:
This is the step the rest of the series hangs on. Each phase of the muscle cell is one current, and each current draws one piece of the ECG. Know which current is disturbed, and you can predict the ECG without memorising it.

Take the phases in order.

Phase zero is sodium, and it draws the QRS. Block the sodium gates and each cell's upstroke becomes slower and weaker. A weaker shove to the next cell means slower conduction through the muscle, so the ventricle takes longer to activate, and the QRS widens. What blocks sodium? The class one antiarrhythmics, such as flecainide and procainamide. Tricyclic antidepressants in overdose. Cocaine. And a high potassium, by a different route: it makes the resting voltage less negative, and sodium gates that never get back to minus ninety stay locked. Different causes, the same wide QRS, because it is the same current.

Phase two is the plateau, calcium, and it is the ST segment. Here the thing that changes is length. A low calcium makes the plateau last longer. So the ST segment stretches, like a longer piece of flat track between the QRS and the T wave. The T wave itself is normal, only pushed later, and the QT is long. A high calcium does the reverse. The plateau is cut short, the ST segment almost disappears, the T wave starts almost straight off the QRS, and the QT is short.

Phase three is potassium, and it draws the T wave. Here there's a fact that sounds backwards, so take it slowly. The potassium channels of phase three work better when there is more potassium outside the cell. So a high potassium speeds phase three. Repolarisation is brisk, and the T wave becomes tall, narrow and peaked, like a tent. A low potassium slows those channels. Phase three drags, the T wave flattens and spreads, and a U wave appears behind it. The interval from the Q wave to the end of that U wave looks long.

The same channel has a drug story. The main phase three current runs through a channel called hERG, and a great many drugs block it: the class three antiarrhythmics such as sotalol and amiodarone, macrolide antibiotics, haloperidol, ondansetron, and a long list besides. Block it and phase three is slow, so the QT lengthens. A cell that lingers near its plateau can let its calcium gates reopen and fire a small extra upstroke, an early afterdepolarisation. That is the spark for torsades de pointes, which gets its own section in the second packet.

[[QRS is sodium. The ST segment is calcium. The T wave is potassium. The QT is the whole cell. Ask which current is disturbed, and the ECG follows.]]

One group is left: the things that act on the calcium cells of the nodes, and not on the muscle. Beta-blockers, verapamil and diltiazem, digoxin, adenosine, the vagus. They slow the sinus rate and lengthen the PR interval. They leave the QRS narrow, because the QRS belongs to sodium cells. So a slow rate and a long PR with a narrow QRS says node. A wide QRS says sodium, whatever the poison.

{{**Phase 0, Na⁺ blocked** (class I, TCA, cocaine, high K⁺) | wide QRS
**Phase 2:** low Ca²⁺ | long ST, long QT, normal T
**Phase 2:** high Ca²⁺ | short ST, short QT
**Phase 3:** high K⁺ | tall, narrow, peaked T
**Phase 3:** low K⁺ | flat T, U wave, long QU
**Phase 3:** IKr block (class III, macrolides, haloperidol, ondansetron) | long QT, torsades
**Nodal drugs** | slow rate, long PR, narrow QRS}}

Now the trap, and NEET sets it often. Two different things make the QT long, and they look different. [[A low calcium lengthens the ST segment and leaves the T wave normal. A low potassium, or a drug that blocks the potassium channel, changes the T wave itself. And a high calcium shortens the QT, so an option saying hypercalcaemia prolongs the QT is false.]] One more pair confuses people: a high potassium gives a tall T wave, but so do the first minutes of a blocked coronary artery. The potassium T wave is narrow and pointed, with a short QT. The ischaemia section shows you the other one, which is broad.

You can now say what each wave means. What you can't yet say is why the same wave is upright in one lead and upside down in another. For that you need the cameras.
lesson.cap: QRS is sodium, ST is calcium, T is potassium, QT is the whole cell.

spine: The node cell climbs by the funny current in phase 4 to about −40 mV, fires on L-type calcium, repolarises on potassium. Phase 4 slope sets the rate.
The SA node's firing is invisible; the P wave is atrial muscle answering.
The ECG records current between cells that disagree: phase 0 (sodium) draws the QRS, the phase 2 plateau is the flat ST, phase 3 (potassium) draws the T.
The T is upright because epicardium repolarises first: opposite charge moving in the opposite direction.
Paper: small square 0.04 s, large square 0.2 s; PR 0.12–0.20 s, QRS under 0.12 s, QTc up to about 450 ms (men) and 460 ms (women).
QRS is sodium, ST is calcium, T is potassium, QT is the whole cell; nodal drugs change rate and PR, not the QRS.

questions.text: Leads as cameras: one rule explains axis, R waves and hypertrophy

open.text:
Axis deviation, R wave progression, bundle branch patterns, Q waves and reciprocal changes are not five topics. They are one rule, used from different viewpoints. A wave of depolarisation coming towards a lead writes upwards. Going away, it writes downwards.

Think of the twelve leads as twelve cameras fixed around one heart. A wave of firing starts at the top right, crosses the atria, waits at the door, and sweeps through the ventricles in a fixed order. Twelve cameras film that one event from twelve positions, and that is the only reason the traces differ.

So this section first puts the cameras in their places. Then it uses the rule three times: to find the axis, which is the average direction of the sweep; to explain why V1 shows a small r and a deep S while V6 shows the opposite; and to see what a bigger chamber does. It ends with healthy hearts that break the picture, and a signal too weak to film.

The trap to listen for is a technical one: two swapped arm electrodes can imitate a heart on the wrong side of the chest.

First, the rule, and where each camera stands.

steps.bridge: Twelve views of one sweep. Next: average the sweep into one arrow, the axis, and see the three reasons it swings.

lesson.text:
One rule. When the wave of depolarisation travels towards a lead, the trace goes up. When it travels away, the trace goes down. When it travels straight across the lead's line of sight, neither towards nor away, the trace goes up and down by equal amounts, and that complex is called equiphasic. The size of the deflection depends on how squarely the wave heads at the camera, and on how much muscle carries it.

Now place the cameras. There are two sets of six.

The first six are the limb leads, and they look at the heart in the frontal plane, as if the chest were a clock face seen from the front. Each is named by an angle. Lead one looks from the left side, at zero degrees. Go downwards from there. Lead two looks from the left hip, at plus sixty degrees. aVF looks from the feet, at plus ninety. Lead three looks from the right hip, at plus one hundred and twenty. Now go upwards from lead one. aVL looks from the left shoulder, at minus thirty. And aVR looks from the right shoulder, at minus one hundred and fifty, on its own on the far side.

Run the normal beat past them. The wave starts at the SA node, top right, and the bulk of the ventricular wave heads down and to the left, towards the left hip. Lead two stands almost exactly there, so it sees everything coming straight at it. That's why lead two has a clear upright P wave and a tall R wave, and why it is the rhythm strip. aVR stands at the right shoulder, behind the starting point, looking into the cavity of the heart. Everything runs away from it. So in a normal ECG the P wave, the QRS and the T wave are all negative in aVR. If aVR is upright, something is wrong with the heart or with the electrodes.

The second six are the chest leads, and they look in the horizontal plane, a ring around the chest at the level of the heart. V1 sits just to the right of the breastbone and V2 just to the left, both in the fourth space, in front of the right ventricle and the septum. V4 is in the fifth space in the midclavicular line, over the apex, and V3 lies between V2 and V4. V5 is level with V4 in the anterior axillary line, and V6 in the mid-axillary line, looking at the side wall of the left ventricle.

{{**Limb leads (frontal):** aVL −30° | lead I 0° | lead II +60° | aVF +90° | lead III +120° | aVR −150°
**Chest leads (horizontal):** V1–V2 right ventricle and septum | V3–V4 anterior | V5–V6 lateral
**Territories:** inferior II, III, aVF | lateral I, aVL, V5, V6 | septal V1, V2 | anterior V3, V4}}

Because each camera stands nearest one wall, the leads group into territories, and you'll use these in every infarct.

[[Lead two, three and aVF look up from below: the inferior wall. Lead one, aVL, V5 and V6 look from the left: the lateral wall. V1 and V2 face the septum. V3 and V4 face the anterior wall.]]

The rule gives you one more idea for free. If one camera sees something coming towards it, the camera on the opposite side sees the same thing going away. It records the mirror image. That is a reciprocal change. aVL, up at the left shoulder, is roughly opposite lead three, so an event that lifts the trace in the inferior leads pushes it down in aVL. And notice that no standard camera stands behind the heart. The back wall of the left ventricle is filmed only from the front, by V1 to V3, in mirror image. The ischaemia section uses that to find the posterior infarct.

Last, the trap from the section opening. Suppose the right arm and left arm electrodes are swapped. Lead one is recorded between the two arms, so it flips completely: an upside down P wave, QRS and T wave in lead one. aVR and aVL change places, so aVR now looks upright. It looks like a heart lying on the right side of the chest. But the chest electrodes haven't moved. With swapped arm electrodes the R wave still grows normally from V1 to V6. In true dextrocardia the heart really is on the right, so the R waves shrink from V1 to V6. One look at the chest leads separates them.

[[An inverted lead one with an upright aVR means either swapped arm electrodes or dextrocardia. Normal R wave growth across the chest leads means the electrodes were swapped.]]

Twelve cameras, one sweep. Now average the sweep into a single arrow.
lesson.cap: One rule: towards the lead = upright, away = downward, perpendicular = equiphasic.

steps.bridge: The limb leads gave one arrow. Now the chest leads: why V1 writes a small r and a deep S, and V6 the opposite.

lesson.text:
Add up every part of the ventricular wave during the QRS and you get one arrow: the average direction in which the ventricles depolarise, seen in the frontal plane. That arrow is the axis. It is the camera rule run backwards: where must the wave be going, for the cameras to see this?

Normally the arrow points down and to the left, towards the left hip, because the left ventricle is the big muscle and it lies down and to the left. Normal runs from minus thirty degrees to plus ninety degrees. More negative than minus thirty is left axis deviation: the arrow has swung up towards the left shoulder. Beyond plus ninety is right axis deviation: the arrow has swung towards the right hip.

You find it with two cameras at right angles: lead one, looking from the left, and aVF, looking from the feet. If the QRS is mainly upright in both, the wave is heading left and down. Normal. If lead one is upright but aVF is negative, the wave is heading left and up. That may or may not be abnormal, because normal extends up to minus thirty. So check lead two. [[With lead one upright and aVF negative, lead two decides: if lead two is still upright the axis is normal, and if lead two is negative it is true left axis deviation.]] Why lead two? Because lead two sits at plus sixty, and the line at right angles to plus sixty is minus thirty. Exactly at minus thirty, lead two would be equiphasic: the perpendicular rule at work.

If lead one is negative and aVF is upright, the wave is heading right and down: right axis deviation. If both are negative, it is heading up towards the right shoulder, the one direction a normal heart never takes. That is the extreme axis, also called the north-west axis. Think of ventricular tachycardia, severe hyperkalaemia or misplaced electrodes.

For a precise answer, find the limb lead where the QRS is most nearly equiphasic. The axis is at right angles to that lead, and the upright leads tell you which of the two directions.

{{**Lead I up, aVF up** | normal
**Lead I up, aVF down** | look at lead II: up = normal, down = **left axis deviation**
**Lead I down, aVF up** | **right axis deviation**
**Lead I down, aVF down** | extreme (north-west) axis
Normal axis −30° to +90°}}

Now the part that makes the cause lists unnecessary.

[[The axis swings for only three reasons: towards extra muscle, away from dead muscle, and towards the region that is activated late.]]

First, towards extra muscle, because more muscle is more current. A thick right ventricle pulls the arrow to the right. A thick left ventricle pulls it a little further left.

Second, away from dead muscle. Dead tissue produces no current, so the opposite wall is unopposed. An inferior infarct removes the downward forces and the arrow tips up and to the left. A lateral infarct removes the leftward forces and the arrow tips to the right.

Third, towards the part that is activated late. If one cable is blocked, the muscle it served is reached late, by the slow route, after everything else has finished. That late, unopposed activity drags the arrow towards itself. Block the left anterior fascicle, which serves the upper front of the left ventricle, and the last activity is up and to the left: left axis deviation. Block the left posterior fascicle and it is down and to the right: right axis deviation.

So sort the lists by those three. Left axis deviation: left anterior fascicular block, the commonest cause; inferior infarction; left ventricular hypertrophy, where the shift is mild; and the exam extras, an ostium primum atrial septal defect and pacing from the right ventricular apex. Right axis deviation: right ventricular hypertrophy; acute right ventricular strain, as in pulmonary embolism; chronic lung disease; lateral infarction; left posterior fascicular block; and the normal child or tall thin adult. A sodium channel blocker shifts only the last part of the QRS to the right, which the poisons section shows you in aVR.

{{**Left axis:** LAFB (commonest), inferior MI, LVH (mild), RV apical pacing, ostium primum ASD, WPW (some), hyperkalaemia, pregnancy (mild)
**Right axis:** RVH, acute PE or RV strain, COPD, lateral MI, LPFB, dextrocardia, arm-lead reversal, children and tall thin adults, sodium-channel blocker toxicity (terminal)}}

NEET's favourite wrong step is to call left axis deviation the moment aVF is negative. Check lead two first.

The axis collapses the limb cameras into one arrow. The chest cameras tell their own story, and it starts with the septum.
lesson.cap: Lead I and aVF both up = normal. I up, aVF down: check lead II — up = normal, down = left axis. I down, aVF up = right axis.

steps.bridge: More muscle means bigger waves. Next: the voltage rules for a thick ventricle, and the two shapes of a big atrium.

lesson.text:
Recall the order: the septum first, from left to right, then the two ventricles together. Now stand at two cameras, V1 beside the breastbone and V6 at the left side of the chest, and watch that order go by.

First the septum. Its wave runs from left to right, and slightly forwards. V1 is on the right and in front, so the wave comes towards it: a small upward blip, a small r. V6 is on the left, so the same wave moves away from it: a small downward blip, a small q. That is called the septal q, and you'll see it in the left-sided cameras: V5, V6, lead one and aVL. It is small, narrow and normal. If the left bundle is blocked, the septum has to fire from right to left, and the septal q vanishes: a sign of left bundle branch block.

Then the ventricles. Both fire at once, the right sending its wave to the right, the left sending its wave to the left and backwards. But the left ventricle has about three times the muscle. The waves add, the left wins, and the net wave runs to the left and back. From V1 that is going away: a deep downward S. From V6 it is coming towards: a tall R. So V1 writes a small r and a deep S. V6 writes a small q and a tall R. Same beat, opposite pictures, one rule.

[[V1 shows a small r and a deep S because the septum fires towards it and then the large left ventricle fires away from it. V6 shows the mirror: a small q and a tall R.]]

Walk the cameras round from V1 to V6. Each stands a little further to the left, so the R wave grows and the S wave shrinks. Where they are equal is the transition zone, normally at V3 or V4. The steady growth is called R wave progression.

Now the number NEET asks. In V1 the R to S ratio is normally less than one. An R taller than the S in V1 of an adult, a dominant R wave, is abnormal until explained. Derive the explanations from the rule: what could send more of the wave towards V1?

More muscle on the right: right ventricular hypertrophy. The right ventricle now out-votes the left.

Late activation on the right: right bundle branch block. The right ventricle fires late and unopposed, after the left has finished, so V1 shows a second R wave after the S, and the QRS is wide.

Loss of muscle at the back: posterior infarction. V1 is the mirror for the back wall. A Q wave at the back appears as a tall, broad R wave at the front. ST elevation at the back appears as ST depression at the front, and the T wave is upright. NEET's trap is to call ST depression with tall R waves in V1 to V3 anterior ischaemia.

Early activation at the back: Wolff-Parkinson-White with a left-sided pathway. The extra connection fires the back of the left ventricle early, and that wave travels forwards, towards V1. The PR interval is short.

A heart on the other side: dextrocardia. Rarer causes are hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where a thick septum exaggerates the first blip; Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which scars the back wall; misplaced chest electrodes; and the normal young child.

{{**Dominant R in V1 (R/S > 1):** RVH | posterior MI (ST depression, upright T in V1–V3) | RBBB (rSR′, wide QRS) | WPW, left-sided pathway (short PR, delta) | dextrocardia | HCM | Duchenne | lead misplacement | normal child
**Poor R progression:** anterior MI | LVH | LBBB | COPD | cardiomyopathy | leads placed too high}}

The opposite problem is poor R wave progression: the R wave fails to grow from V1 to V3 or V4. Again the rule gives the causes. Dead muscle at the front, an old anterior infarct, so nothing comes towards those cameras. A thick left ventricle or a left bundle branch block, where the forces running back and left swamp the early forward ones. Chronic lung disease, where overinflated lungs push the heart down and turn it. And electrodes placed too high. So poor R wave progression alone never proves an old infarct.

Clockwise and counterclockwise rotation are only names for where the transition falls. Late, at V5 or V6, is clockwise. Early, at V2, is counterclockwise.

[[A dominant R wave in V1 means right ventricular hypertrophy, posterior infarction, right bundle branch block, a left-sided accessory pathway or dextrocardia.]]

A dominant R wave from extra muscle brings us to what a bigger chamber does to all the cameras.
lesson.cap: Septum fires left to right first (small r in V1, small q in V6); then the big LV pulls away from V1. Transition at V3–V4.

steps.bridge: Not every odd ECG is disease. Next: the child, the pregnant woman, the athlete and the mirror-image heart.

lesson.text:
The camera rule has a second half that we've only touched. The size of a deflection depends on how much muscle is producing it. A thicker ventricle makes taller waves in the cameras that face it and deeper waves in the cameras opposite. That is all the hypertrophy criteria are. The numbers are only where people drew the line.

The left ventricle first. A thick left ventricle sends a bigger wave to the left and back. V5 and V6 face it, so their R waves grow. V1 is opposite, so its S wave deepens. [[The oldest rule, the Sokolow-Lyon criterion, simply adds the two: the S wave in V1 plus the taller R wave of V5 or V6, thirty-five millimetres or more.]] The Cornell criterion uses one camera from each plane: the R wave in aVL plus the S wave in V3, more than twenty-eight millimetres in men and more than twenty in women. An R wave in aVL of more than eleven millimetres also counts on its own.

Voltage is not the whole story. A thick wall takes longer to activate, and its recovery then runs in the wrong direction. You see the result in the lateral leads, V5, V6, lead one and aVL: the ST segment slopes downwards into an inverted, lopsided T wave, with a slow descent and a quicker return. That is the strain pattern. It is called a secondary change, because it follows from the abnormal QRS and not from a diseased artery. Add a mild leftward axis and signs of a big left atrium, and the picture is complete.

One warning. The voltage rules are specific but not sensitive, and they mislead in the young and the thin, whose cameras sit close to the heart. Tall voltage alone in a fit twenty-year-old isn't hypertrophy. Echo decides, as you saw in the Shock packets.

Now the right ventricle. Normally it is out-voted, so a thick right ventricle has to overturn the normal picture before it shows. The axis swings to the right. V1 gets a dominant R wave, seven millimetres or more, and taller than its S wave. V5 and V6 get deep S waves, because the wave is now leaving them. And a right-sided strain pattern appears where the right ventricle faces the cameras: ST depression and T inversion in V1 to V3, and often in the inferior leads.

Then the atria. The P wave is two atria, one after the other. The SA node is in the right atrium, so the right atrium fires first and makes the first half of the P wave. The left atrium is reached later and makes the second half. That one fact explains both abnormal P waves.

Enlarge the right atrium and the first half gets bigger. But it still finishes before the left atrium has finished, so the P wave is no longer than before. It is taller: a peaked P wave of more than two and a half millimetres in lead two, three and aVF. That is P pulmonale, and the name gives you the cause: lung disease and pulmonary hypertension.

Enlarge the left atrium and the second half gets bigger and later. Now the P wave is longer: more than zero point one two seconds in lead two, with two humps, like the letter M. And because the left atrium lies at the back of the heart, its wave travels away from V1. So in V1 the P wave ends in a deep, wide downward dip. That is P mitrale, and its classic cause is mitral stenosis.

[[A big right atrium makes the P wave tall and peaked, over two and a half millimetres: P pulmonale. A big left atrium makes it wide and notched, over zero point one two seconds, with a deep negative end in V1: P mitrale.]]

{{**LVH:** S V1 + R V5 or V6 ≥ 35 mm (Sokolow-Lyon) | R aVL + S V3 > 28 mm men, > 20 mm women (Cornell) | R aVL > 11 mm | strain in V5, V6, I, aVL
**RVH:** right axis | R in V1 ≥ 7 mm, R/S > 1 | deep S in V5, V6 | strain V1–V3
**P pulmonale:** > 2.5 mm, peaked, II, III, aVF | **P mitrale:** > 0.12 s, notched; deep terminal negative P in V1}}

Put several together and you have the ECG of chronic obstructive lung disease: P pulmonale, a rightward axis, low voltage because air lies between the heart and the cameras, poor R wave progression, and sometimes multifocal atrial tachycardia.

Keep the strain pattern in mind: ST depression and T inversion from thick muscle, not from a narrowed artery, are the first of the ischaemia mimics. Before that, a few hearts that are healthy and still break these rules.
lesson.cap: LVH: S V1 + R V5/6 ≥ 35 mm, lateral strain. RVH: dominant R V1, right axis. P pulmonale tall (> 2.5 mm); P mitrale wide and notched (> 0.12 s).

steps.bridge: Tall or oddly aimed waves can be normal. Last in this section: waves that are too small, and a QRS that alternates.

lesson.text:
Every rule so far described an adult with a heart in the usual place. Four kinds of healthy person don't fit, and you can already explain each.

The child. Before birth the right ventricle does at least as much work as the left, pumping to the body through the duct. So a newborn has a thick right ventricle, and the ECG shows what a thick right ventricle always shows: a rightward axis, anywhere up to about plus one hundred and eighty degrees, and a dominant R wave in V1. Over the first years the left ventricle takes over. The heart is also small and fast. A newborn's rate is about one hundred and ten to one hundred and sixty, and the PR interval and the QRS are shorter than an adult's, because the road is shorter. The rate rising and falling with breathing, sinus arrhythmia, is normal.

The T waves need care. For the first few days of life the T wave in V1 is upright. After the first week it turns negative, and the T waves in V1 to V3 stay inverted through childhood, until adolescence. That is the juvenile T wave pattern. NEET's trap is the reverse. An upright T wave in V1, in a child between one week of age and adolescence, suggests right ventricular hypertrophy.

[[T wave inversion in V1 to V3 is normal from the first week of life until adolescence. In that age range it is the upright T wave in V1 that is abnormal, and it suggests right ventricular hypertrophy.]]

Pregnancy. The growing uterus pushes the diaphragm up, and the heart is tilted upwards and to the left. Tilt the heart and you tilt the arrow: a mild leftward shift of the axis. Lead three now looks at the heart from a slightly different angle, so it can show a small Q wave and an inverted T wave, and these change with breathing as the diaphragm moves. The heart rate rises by ten to twenty a minute. Minor ST and T wave changes and extra beats are common, and none of this is disease.

The athlete. Training enlarges the heart and raises resting vagal tone. Remember where the vagus has its grip: the two nodes. So the athlete shows vagal findings at the nodes: sinus bradycardia, a long PR interval, and even Mobitz one block at rest, all of which disappear with exercise. The larger ventricle gives tall QRS voltage on its own, without strain. And early repolarisation, a lifted J point with an upward curving ST segment, is common. All of these are normal in an athlete.

What training does not cause is the important half. T wave inversion beyond V2. Pathological Q waves. Left bundle branch block. The Brugada pattern. And the epsilon wave, a small notch just after the QRS in V1 that points to a right ventricular cardiomyopathy. Those need investigation. There is one accepted exception: a lifted J point and a domed ST segment, followed by T inversion in V1 to V4. The International Criteria of twenty seventeen call it the Black athlete's repolarisation variant. The twenty twenty-six revision keeps it as a normal finding and renames it the anterior early repolarisation pattern, without a label of race. T inversion in V1 to V3 is also accepted in an athlete younger than sixteen.

[[In an athlete, sinus bradycardia, first degree block, Mobitz one at rest, early repolarisation and tall voltage alone are normal. T inversion beyond V2, Q waves, left bundle branch block, epsilon waves and the Brugada pattern are not.]]

Dextrocardia. The heart is a mirror image, lying in the right chest, so every camera on the left is looking at it from the wrong side. Lead one is upside down throughout: P wave, QRS and T wave. aVR is upright. And across the chest the R wave gets smaller from V1 to V6, because the cameras are walking away from the heart. Swapped arm leads look the same; the chest leads decide. Shrinking R waves mean the heart really is on the right, and if you move the chest electrodes to the right side of the chest, the normal progression reappears.

{{**Child:** right axis, dominant R in V1, T inverted V1–V3 until adolescence, rate 110–160 in the newborn
**Pregnancy:** mild left axis shift, rate up 10–20, small Q and inverted T in lead III
**Athlete, normal:** sinus bradycardia, first-degree block, Mobitz I at rest, early repolarisation, voltage alone
**Dextrocardia:** lead I inverted, aVR upright, R shrinks V1 to V6}}

So waves that are tall, or pointing an unusual way, can be normal. The last step is the opposite: waves that are too small.

steps.bridge: The normal machine is built. Next: a blocked artery, and what injured muscle does to the flat ST segment.

lesson.text:
A camera can only film what reaches it. The QRS you measure on the skin is the heart's current after it has crossed the pericardium, the lung and the chest wall. So a small QRS has only two possible explanations. Something is lying between the heart and the cameras, or the heart is producing less current.

First the definition. Low voltage means the whole QRS, from top to bottom, is less than five millimetres in every limb lead, or less than ten millimetres in every chest lead. Either one is enough.

Take the first mechanism: something in the way. Fluid, air and fat all damp the signal. Fluid is a pericardial or pleural effusion, or severe generalised oedema. Air is the overinflated chest of chronic obstructive lung disease, or a pneumothorax. Fat is obesity.

The second mechanism: less current from the muscle, because muscle has been replaced by something that doesn't fire. The classic is amyloid, where protein is laid down between the muscle cells. And here is a pairing the examiners love. On echo, the walls of an amyloid heart are thick. On the ECG, the voltage is low. A truly thick muscle gives high voltage, as the hypertrophy step showed. Thick walls with low voltage means the thickness isn't muscle. The other causes on this side are a heart that has lost a great deal of muscle to infarction, and severe hypothyroidism.

Hypothyroidism deserves its own picture, because it uses both mechanisms. A low thyroid level flattens the pacemaker slope, so there is sinus bradycardia. It often causes a pericardial effusion, so there is low voltage. And repolarisation is slowed, so the T waves are flat or inverted and the QT is long. A slow, small, flat ECG in a cold, drowsy patient is myxoedema.

[[Low voltage is a QRS under five millimetres in every limb lead or under ten in every chest lead. Either something lies between the heart and the leads, such as fluid, air or fat, or the muscle has been replaced, as in amyloid.]]

{{**Low voltage:** QRS < 5 mm in all limb leads or < 10 mm in all chest leads
**Something in the way:** pericardial effusion, pleural effusion, COPD, pneumothorax, obesity, anasarca
**Less muscle current:** amyloid (thick walls on echo), myxoedema, extensive infarction, constriction
**Tamponade on ECG:** sinus tachycardia + low voltage + electrical alternans}}

Now the sign that belongs to a large pericardial effusion. When the sac holds a lot of fluid, the heart is no longer held in place. It swings like a weight hanging in water, forwards on one beat and back on the next. So on one beat it is nearer the chest cameras, and on the next it is further away. The QRS comes out taller, then shorter, then taller, alternating beat by beat, and its axis can shift with it. That is electrical alternans. Nothing is wrong with conduction. The heart is simply moving in front of the cameras.

Put three findings together: sinus tachycardia, low voltage and electrical alternans. That is tamponade on the ECG. Alternans is specific but insensitive: it means a great deal when present, but most patients with tamponade don't show it. When the P wave alternates as well as the QRS, which is called total alternans, tamponade is close to certain. The pressures, the pulsus paradoxus and the drainage come in the Pericardium packet. The picture to carry there is a heart swinging in fluid.

One name to keep apart. T wave alternans is a different thing. There the QRS is steady, and the T wave changes its size or direction from one beat to the next. It has nothing to do with fluid. It means repolarisation is unstable, it is seen in the long QT syndromes, and it scores in the Schwartz criteria that the second packet teaches. An alternating QRS is a swinging heart. An alternating T wave is an unstable cell.

[[Electrical alternans is the QRS height alternating beat to beat because the heart swings in a large effusion. With sinus tachycardia and low voltage it means tamponade. T wave alternans is different: unstable repolarisation in long QT.]]

You now have the whole normal machine: the relay, the two kinds of cell, the phases and the cameras. Everything from here is that machine under attack. The first attack is a blocked artery, and the question is what injured muscle does to that flat ST segment.
lesson.cap: Low voltage: < 5 mm in limb leads, < 10 mm in chest leads. Alternans + sinus tachycardia + low voltage = think tamponade.

spine: One rule: a wave coming towards a lead writes up, going away writes down, crossing at right angles is equiphasic. Twelve leads are twelve cameras on one sweep.
Axis is the average direction (normal −30° to +90°): lead I and aVF first, lead II settles a negative aVF. It swings towards muscle, away from infarct, towards late activation.
Septum fires left to right, then the big left ventricle: V1 small r, deep S; V6 small q, tall R; transition at V3–V4.
Dominant R in V1: RVH, posterior MI (mirror), RBBB, left-sided WPW, dextrocardia. More muscle means more voltage: Sokolow-Lyon 35 mm, Cornell 28/20 mm.
P pulmonale is tall (over 2.5 mm); P mitrale is wide and notched (over 0.12 s). Children, pregnancy and athletes have their own normal.
Low voltage: something between heart and leads, or muscle replaced. Alternating QRS with sinus tachycardia and low voltage is a heart swinging in tamponade.

questions.text: Ischaemia through the cameras: injury current, territories and the hidden infarcts

open.text:
ST elevation and ST depression are not two different diseases. They are one current, seen by cameras standing on opposite sides of it.

You've built the wiring, turned two action potentials into the waves, and placed twelve cameras around the heart with one rule: towards the camera is up, away from it is down. Until now the heart in front of those cameras was healthy. Now a coronary artery closes, and you watch what each camera records.

Four questions, in order. Why does injured muscle move the ST segment at all, when the plateau should keep it flat? How much movement counts? Whose artery is it? And then the infarcts that the standard twelve leads can't see, or show in disguise: the back wall, the right ventricle, the left main, and a closing artery that announces itself with nothing but a T wave.

Listen for two traps. One is a pain-free patient with a normal troponin whose T waves say the big anterior artery is about to shut. The other is an inferior infarct in which a nitrate drops the pressure through the floor.

Begin with the current itself.

steps.bridge: The ST segment shifts towards injured muscle. Where exactly do you measure the shift, and how much counts?

lesson.text:
Go back to phase two, the plateau. During it every ventricular cell sits at about the same voltage. No difference between cells means no current, and the pen rests on the baseline. That is the flat ST segment. Phase four is the same: every cell rests at minus ninety millivolts, so the line between the T wave and the next P wave is flat too.

Now starve one patch of muscle. Holding minus ninety at rest, and holding a full plateau, both cost ATP. A cell without oxygen runs short, and two things follow. Potassium leaks out, so the cell can't get back down to minus ninety and rests nearer minus seventy. And potassium channels that ATP normally holds shut swing open, so its plateau is lower and shorter.

So the injured patch now differs from its healthy neighbours twice in every beat, at rest and during the plateau. Wherever neighbouring regions sit at different voltages, a current flows across the border. This is the injury current. During the plateau it pushes the ST segment towards the injured patch. At rest it drags the baseline the other way, which the machine, redrawing the baseline as zero, also shows as an ST shift towards the patch.

[[Injured muscle can't hold its resting potential or its plateau, so a current flows across its border with healthy muscle. On the ECG the ST segment shifts towards the injured region.]]

Now apply the one rule of the cameras. If the injury runs through the full thickness of the wall, it reaches the outer surface, directly under the camera. The shift points at that camera: ST elevation. The camera on the opposite side of the heart sees the same shift pointing away, and records ST depression. That is the reciprocal view you've met. It is not a second problem. It is the same injury seen from behind.

If the injury is confined to the inner layer, the subendocardium, the picture turns over. The inner layer is the last to be fed and the hardest squeezed, so it suffers first when an artery is narrowed but not closed. Now the injured zone lies on the far side of healthy muscle from every camera on the chest. The shift points inward, at the cavity, away from all of them: ST depression. Only aVR, looking into the cavity from the right shoulder, sees it coming and records elevation. So ST elevation tells you which wall. This kind of ST depression does not. It gathers in the lateral leads whichever artery is narrowed, and NEET's wrong option is to name the artery from it.

Next, time. An occlusion writes a sequence. Within minutes the T wave over the patch grows tall and broad: the hyperacute T wave. Leaked potassium pools around those cells, and you know that high potassium makes a tall T. Unlike true hyperkalaemia it is broad at the base and confined to one territory. Then the ST segment rises, over minutes to hours. Over hours, Q waves appear. Dead muscle makes no electricity, so it acts as a window. The camera looks straight through it and records the far wall depolarising away from it: a downward wave at the very start of the QRS. Then the T wave inverts, and over days to about two weeks the ST segment settles to the baseline. The Q wave stays for life.

{{**After an occlusion**
Minutes | hyperacute T: tall, broad
Minutes to hours | ST elevation
Hours | Q waves
Hours to days | T inversion
Days to 2 weeks | ST back to baseline; Q stays
ST still up at weeks | LV aneurysm
**Pathological Q:** ≥ 0.04 s or > 25% of R; in V2–V3 any Q > 0.02 s; UDMI elsewhere: ≥ 0.03 s and ≥ 1 mm deep}}

One number, last. In the classic teaching a Q wave is pathological when it is at least zero point zero four seconds wide, or deeper than a quarter of the R wave after it. In V2 and V3 the Universal Definition counts any Q wave wider than zero point zero two seconds. In the other leads its cut is zero point zero three seconds wide and at least one millimetre deep, in two neighbouring leads. So if an option says zero point zero three, that is the Universal Definition, and zero point zero four is the older textbook answer. The small lateral q waves are the septum, and normal.

[[The infarct evolves in order: hyperacute T, ST elevation, Q waves, T inversion, then the ST settles. Q waves are permanent. ST elevation that persists for weeks is an aneurysm.]]

Where on the tracing you measure the shift, and how much counts, comes next.
lesson.cap: Transmural injury lifts the ST in the leads that face it; subendocardial injury depresses it. Order: hyperacute T, ST elevation, Q, T inversion; the Q stays.

steps.bridge: The elevation is real and big enough to count. Now the most examined question: whose territory?

lesson.text:
Every ST shift is measured at the J point. You met it on the paper: the corner where the QRS ends and the ST segment begins. Why there, and not a little later? Because it is the one fixed landmark. From the J point onward the segment climbs into the T wave, so the later you measure, the more elevation you find.

Measured against what? Against a stretch where the heart is electrically silent. The truest one is the TP segment, the flat line between the end of the T wave and the next P wave. At fast rates that line disappears, so in practice, and on your card, you use the level of the PR segment where the QRS takes off. Keep one exception for the next section: in pericarditis the PR segment is itself pushed down, and then only the TP segment is honest.

How many leads? Two contiguous leads, meaning two neighbouring cameras that look at the same wall: lead two and aVF, or V3 and V4. One lead on its own can be a loose electrode. Two neighbours that agree are an injury current in one territory.

Now the threshold, reason first. In most leads a healthy heart shows almost nothing at the J point, so the bar is low: one millimetre. V2 and V3 are different. They sit closest to the heart, and you remember the notch at the start of the plateau, deeper in the outer layer of muscle than in the inner. For that moment the two layers differ in voltage, and a small upward step appears at the J point in a perfectly healthy heart. It shows best in V2 and V3. It is largest in young men, smaller in older men, and smallest in women. The thresholds are simply set above what is normal for each group.

{{**J-point elevation, two contiguous leads**
V2–V3, men under 40 | **2.5 mm**
V2–V3, men 40 and over | **2.0 mm**
V2–V3, women | **1.5 mm**
All other leads | **1 mm**
Not valid in LBBB or LVH}}

So in V2 and V3: two point five millimetres for men under forty, two millimetres for men of forty and over, one point five millimetres for women of any age. One millimetre everywhere else.

[[ST elevation is measured at the J point in two contiguous leads. One millimetre in most leads. In V2 and V3: two point five for men under forty, two for men forty and over, one point five for women.]]

Two exclusions. The rule is not valid in left bundle branch block or in left ventricular hypertrophy. You saw why with the strain pattern: when depolarisation is abnormal, repolarisation follows it abnormally, and the ST segment is displaced with no injury at all. The bundle has its own criteria, and you'll build them in the next packet.

NEET sets its traps at the edges. A man aged exactly forty uses two millimetres, not two point five. And an option that measures eighty milliseconds after the J point is describing an exercise test, not the Universal Definition.

So an injury current is there, and it is big enough to count. Whose territory is it?
lesson.cap: Measure ST at the J point against the TP baseline. V2–V3: 2 mm men ≥ 40, 2.5 mm men < 40, 1.5 mm women; 1 mm elsewhere, two contiguous leads.

steps.bridge: The map has two blind spots: the back of the heart and the right ventricle.

lesson.text:
You already own this map. You just haven't laid the arteries on it. You grouped the leads by the wall each one faces. Lead two, three and aVF look up from the feet at the inferior wall. Lead one and aVL, with V5 and V6, look from the left at the lateral wall. V1 and V2 sit over the septum, V3 and V4 over the anterior wall.

Now the arteries. The left anterior descending artery, the LAD, runs down the front of the heart in the groove over the septum, sending branches into the septum and across the anterior wall. So V1 to V4 are the LAD. The circumflex runs round the left side, so the lateral leads are the circumflex, with one refinement: the high lateral pair, lead one and aVL, is often a diagonal branch of the LAD. The inferior wall belongs to whichever artery turns the corner at the back and gives the posterior descending branch. In eight or nine people out of ten that is the right coronary. In the rest it is the circumflex.

{{**II, III, aVF** | inferior | **RCA** (III > II) or LCx (II ≥ III)
**I, aVL, V5–V6** | lateral | **LCx**, or diagonal of LAD
**V1–V4** | septal, anterior | **LAD**
V1 elevation + new RBBB | **proximal LAD**
Q waves, flat ST | **old infarct**}}

That raises NEET's first question: an inferior infarct, right coronary or circumflex? Use the angles you learned. Lead three sits at plus one hundred and twenty degrees, so it looks at the inferior wall from the right. Lead two sits at plus sixty, and looks from the left. The right coronary's territory lies to the right, so its injury current points more at lead three. And aVL, at minus thirty degrees, stands almost directly opposite lead three, so it records the mirror image: reciprocal ST depression. More elevation in lead three than in lead two, with depression in aVL, is the right coronary. If lead two matches or beats lead three, and the lateral leads rise as well, it is the circumflex. The wrong option reverses the two leads.

[[Inferior infarct with more ST elevation in lead three than lead two, and reciprocal depression in aVL, is the right coronary. Lead two equal or greater, with lateral elevation, is the circumflex.]]

And from that mirror: ST depression in aVL can be the first visible sign of an inferior infarct. Don't file it as a lateral problem.

Second, what the right coronary carries with it. Go back to the wiring. It feeds the sinus node in about six people in ten and the AV node in about nine in ten. So an inferior infarct brings a slow sinus rate and block at the AV node. Because that block sits in the node itself, among the slow calcium cells, the back-up pacemaker just below it takes over with a narrow QRS at a tolerable rate, and it usually recovers. Hold that thought, because it is half of the next packet. The proximal right coronary also feeds the right ventricle, which is the next card.

Third, how high up the LAD. Its first septal branch supplies the right bundle branch. So ST elevation in V1 together with a new right bundle branch block means the artery is shut near its origin, above that branch. Marrow has asked this twice. It means a large infarct and a high risk of shock.

Fourth, the question most people lost. A breathless man with known coronary disease has Q waves in lead one, aVL and V5, and a flat ST segment. Fewer than half answered it. The tempting option is acute coronary syndrome. But you know the sequence now. The Q wave is the window through dead muscle, and it is permanent. The acute stage is written in the ST segment, and here the ST segment is silent. This is an old lateral infarct.

[[ST elevation in V1 with a new right bundle branch block is a proximal LAD occlusion. Pathological Q waves with a flat ST segment are an old infarct, not an acute one.]]

What you do about a fresh occlusion, primary PCI and its clock, belongs to the ACS packets.

Now look at what the map leaves out. No camera stands behind the heart, and none faces the right ventricle. Two infarcts can hide there.
lesson.cap: Inferior II, III, aVF (RCA); lateral I, aVL, V5–V6 (LCx); septal and anterior V1–V4 (LAD). Reciprocal pairs: inferior ↔ aVL; posterior ↔ V1–V3.

steps.bridge: Two walls hid because no camera faced them. Next, ischaemia that is everywhere at once.

lesson.text:
Start with the wall that no camera faces. The posterior wall of the left ventricle lies against the back, and all six chest leads sit in front. So how do you see an injury there?

In the mirror. V1, V2 and V3 look at the front of the heart, directly opposite the back wall, so whatever the back wall does they record upside down. Run the sequence of an infarct through that mirror. Posterior ST elevation appears in V1 to V3 as ST depression. The posterior Q wave appears as a tall R wave. And the posterior T inversion appears as an upright T. You've met that tall R before: posterior infarction was on your list of causes of a dominant R wave in V1. Here is why it was there.

So with ongoing pain, flat ST depression deepest in V1 to V3, ending in an upright T wave, is a posterior occlusion until shown otherwise.

You prove it by putting cameras where they were missing. Carry the electrodes round the back at the same level as V6. V7 on the posterior axillary line. V8 in line with the tip of the shoulder blade. V9 beside the spine. The threshold there is only half a millimetre, because those leads are far from the heart, behind lung and muscle, and record small voltages. The usual artery is the circumflex, and circumflex occlusions are the ones a standard ECG misses most.

{{**Posterior MI:** V1–V3 ST depression, tall R, upright T
V7 posterior axillary | V8 mid-scapular | V9 paraspinal
ST elevation **≥ 0.5 mm** (men under 40: 1 mm); usually **LCx**
**RV MI:** V4R = right mid-clavicular line, 5th space
ST elevation **≥ 1 mm** (UDMI accepts 0.5); **proximal RCA**}}

[[Posterior infarction shows in V1 to V3 as ST depression with a tall R and an upright T. Confirm it with half a millimetre of ST elevation in V7 to V9. The usual artery is the circumflex.]]

NEET's wrong option calls it anterior ischaemia, because that is where the changes are, and a closed artery is left to wait.

Now the right ventricle. No standard lead faces its free wall, so you make one. V4R is the mirror of V4: the right mid-clavicular line in the fifth intercostal space. One millimetre of ST elevation there strongly suggests right ventricular infarction. The Universal Definition accepts half a millimetre, or one millimetre in men under thirty. The elevation is brief, gone in about half of patients within ten to twelve hours, so record V4R early in every inferior infarct. Two hints in the standard leads say the same: more elevation in lead three than lead two, and elevation in V1, which sits over the right ventricle.
