The branches to the right ventricle leave the right coronary high up, so the right ventricle infarcts only when the occlusion is proximal. Marrow's incorrect statement was that the shock is due to a distal occlusion.

Now the physiology, because this is where you left a question blank. The right ventricle is a thin-walled pump that passes blood through the lungs to the left side. Infarcted, it becomes a passive pipe. Blood crosses the lungs only if the venous filling pressure behind it pushes it across. So three things appear together: low blood pressure, because the left ventricle is underfilled; a raised jugular pressure, because blood is dammed back; and clear lungs, because little reaches them. Everything now depends on preload, a reasonable heart rate, and the atrium contracting in step.

The grand test stem: a man of fifty-eight, ninety minutes of chest pain, ST elevation in lead two, three, aVF and V4R, pulse fifty-four, blood pressure eighty-two over fifty-six, clear lungs, raised jugular pressure. The answer was a cautious crystalloid bolus while primary PCI is arranged. Each wrong option removes something this patient is living on. Nitroglycerin dilates the veins and takes away the filling pressure. Furosemide does the same more slowly. Metoprolol slows a heart that is already slow and depresses an AV node that the same artery supplies.

[[Inferior infarct with ST elevation in V4R, low pressure and clear lungs is a right ventricular infarct from a proximal right coronary occlusion. Give cautious fluid and reperfuse. Avoid nitrates, diuretics and beta-blockers.]]

Those two walls hid because no camera faced them. Next, every camera is looking, and the injury is everywhere at once.
lesson.cap: Posterior MI shows in the mirror: tall R + ST depression + upright T in V1–V3. Confirm in V7–V9 (≥ 0.5 mm). RV infarct: ST elevation in V4R.

steps.bridge: Deep T inversion in the chest leads of a pain-free patient has a name, and it cost you a mark.

lesson.text:
Return to the second half of the injury current. When only the inner layer of the wall is injured, the ST shift points into the cavity, the outside cameras record depression, and aVR records elevation. Now ask what happens when the inner layer of the whole left ventricle is short of blood at the same moment. That is a tight left main stem, or severe disease in all three arteries.

The answer is the same picture, spread across the whole tracing. ST depression of one millimetre or more in many leads, usually deepest in the lateral and inferior leads, with ST elevation in aVR, in V1, or in both. How many leads? The European guideline of twenty twenty-three and the Universal Definition say six or more. Older keys say eight. If a stem says eight, don't argue with it. Six is the current number.

[[ST depression of at least one millimetre in six or more leads, with ST elevation in aVR or V1, is ischaemia of the whole inner layer: left main or severe three-vessel disease.]]

Be exact about what this pattern is. It is not one wall shut off. It is global ischaemia of the inner layer, and that is why the elevation sits only in the one lead that looks into the cavity. With pain or a falling blood pressure it sends the patient for angiography urgently. And because it is a pattern of supply against demand, a ventricle with fixed narrowings can draw it whenever demand outruns supply: a very fast rhythm, severe anaemia, profound hypoxia, the minutes after a cardiac arrest. In the ICU, read it together with the story.

Now the everyday ECG of a narrowed artery that hasn't closed, the non-ST-elevation syndromes. Two changes count. The first is ST depression of half a millimetre or more, in two contiguous leads, that runs flat or slopes downward. The shape matters. At fast heart rates the J point dips and the segment climbs steeply back up, and that upsloping depression is usually innocent. Usually. One upsloping pattern is the dangerous exception, and it is the very next card.

The second change is T wave inversion, deeper than one millimetre, in leads with a tall R wave. Why would ischaemia turn the T wave over? You learned that the normal T wave is upright because the outer layer repolarises first, so repolarisation runs the opposite way to depolarisation. An ischaemic region repolarises late. The order changes, and the T wave points away from that region.

{{**Left main or three-vessel:** ST depression ≥ 1 mm in ≥ 6 leads (older keys: 8) + ST elevation in aVR and/or V1
**NSTE-ACS:** ST depression ≥ 0.5 mm, horizontal or downsloping
T inversion > 1 mm in leads with R/S > 1
A normal ECG does not exclude infarction}}

And there is a third possibility, the one the banks test most: nothing at all. A narrowed artery may leave the tracing completely normal. Chest pain, a normal ECG and a troponin that rises is still an infarct, and the wrong option in each of those questions is unstable angina. How troponin decides that is the business of the first ACS packet. Here you need only the principle.

[[Without ST elevation the ECG may show flat or downsloping ST depression, T inversion, or nothing. A normal ECG never excludes an infarct.]]

One fine point from Marrow. T wave flattening, or inversion of less than a millimetre, in leads with a dominant R wave is a weak sign and counts for little. New ST shift of a millimetre, or T inversion across several chest leads, counts for a lot.

Deep T inversion across the chest leads, in a patient whose pain has gone. Hold that picture, because it has a name.
lesson.cap: ST depression ≥ 1 mm in ≥ 6 leads + ST elevation in aVR and/or V1 = left main or three-vessel ischaemia.

steps.bridge: Infarcts that hide, done. Now the reverse: ST elevation where no artery is closed.

lesson.text:
Two famous patterns turn out to be one artery caught at two moments. Both are the LAD near its origin. In de Winter's pattern it is shut. In Wellens' pattern it has shut, and reopened by itself, for now.

Take Wellens first, because it cost you a mark. Picture the sequence. A plaque high in the LAD ruptures and a clot closes the artery. The patient has chest pain. Then the body's own clot-dissolving system opens it again. The pain goes. No muscle has died, so the R waves are intact, there are no Q waves, and the troponin is normal or only slightly raised. What remains on the ECG is the footprint of reperfusion. You saw it in the sequence of an infarct: after the injury, the T wave inverts.

So the Wellens pattern is deep, symmetric T wave inversion in V2 and V3, sometimes spreading from V1 out to V6, recorded while the patient is free of pain, with little or no ST elevation. That deep symmetric form is the common one, about three quarters of cases. In the other quarter the T wave is biphasic, up first and then down.

The danger is what it predicts. The plaque is still there, the narrowing is critical, and the artery will close again. In the original series, three in four of the patients treated with drugs alone went on to a large anterior infarct within weeks. So the answer is admission and early coronary angiography, in practice within about a day. The European guideline of twenty twenty-three lists the Wellens sign under the non-ST-elevation syndromes, as prominent negative T waves from a severe proximal LAD stenosis.

The grand test stem was exactly this: pain-free, deep symmetric T inversion in V2 and V3, normal troponin. NEET's wrong options are the reassuring ones. Discharge, because the troponin is normal. Or an exercise test to see whether it's really the heart. A stress test is contraindicated here: you would be raising demand through an artery that is one clot away from closing.

[[Pain-free patient, recent angina, deep symmetric or biphasic T waves in V2 and V3, troponin normal or nearly so: Wellens. It is a critical proximal LAD stenosis. Admit for early angiography. Never a stress test.]]

One more behaviour. If the pain returns and the inverted T waves suddenly stand upright again, that is not recovery. The artery has closed again, and ST elevation follows.

Now de Winter. Same artery, but this time it is shut and staying shut, and the patient is in pain. You would expect ST elevation across the chest leads. In about two in every hundred LAD occlusions it doesn't come. The J point is depressed by one to three millimetres in the chest leads, and from that low start the ST segment climbs steeply into a tall, symmetric T wave. There is often a millimetre or two of ST elevation in aVR. So it is upsloping ST depression with tall T waves, and it persists until the artery is opened.

Upsloping depression is usually innocent, which is exactly why de Winter is missed. What gives it away is the tall, symmetric T wave it runs into, and a patient with ongoing chest pain. This is treated as a STEMI: immediate angiography and primary PCI, without waiting for a troponin. The European guideline of twenty twenty-three includes it among the ECG patterns that should send a patient for immediate reperfusion.

{{**Wellens** | pain-free | deep symmetric (about 75%) or biphasic T in V2–V3; no Q, R preserved; troponin normal or slightly up | critical LAD stenosis | **early angiography, no stress test**
**de Winter** | in pain | upsloping ST depression 1–3 mm + tall symmetric T in V1–V6; aVR up 1–2 mm | **LAD occluded** | **immediate PCI**}}

[[de Winter: ongoing pain, upsloping ST depression running into tall symmetric T waves in the chest leads. It is an occluded LAD without ST elevation. Reperfuse immediately.]]

One discriminator separates the two. Wellens is the pain-free, reopened artery. De Winter is the painful, closed one.

You've now seen infarcts that hide. Finish this section with the reverse: ST elevation where no artery is closed at all.
lesson.cap: Wellens (pain-free, T biphasic or deeply inverted in V2–V3) = critical LAD, angiography. de Winter (in pain, upsloping ST depression + tall T) = occluded LAD, reperfuse now.

steps.bridge: If the ST segment only reports a voltage difference between neighbours, what else can create one?

lesson.text:
The number tells you the ST segment is up. The shape, and the company it keeps, tell you whether to believe it. Four patterns lift the ST segment, and you can now derive each one.

Begin with the real one. In a STEMI the injury goes through the wall, and the ST segment is pulled up into the T wave until the two form a single dome. The curve is convex upward, like a frown. Three things travel with it, and you've built all three. It is confined to one arterial territory. The camera opposite shows reciprocal depression. And it evolves over hours, growing Q waves and inverting its T wave while the segment is still raised.

Early repolarisation is the healthy impostor. Go back to the notch at the start of the plateau, deeper in the outer layer of the wall than in the inner. In some people, mostly young men and athletes, that difference is pronounced, and it draws a small notch or slur at the J point with the segment lifting off it in a curve that is concave upward, like a smile. In V4 the notch gives the J point a fish-hook look. Nothing is injured. So there is no territory, no reciprocal depression, and no change from hour to hour or year to year.

Pericarditis is concave as well, but the inflammation wraps the whole heart, so the elevation is widespread and respects no artery. And it has one feature the others lack, a depressed PR segment. Why an inflamed sac should move the ST segment at all is the first question of the next section.

Left bundle branch block is the fourth. There the ST segment simply points away from the main QRS deflection, which is called discordance. It is the expected result of abnormal depolarisation and not an injury. You'll see how an infarct is found through that disguise when you reach the bundle branches.

{{**STEMI** | convex, one territory, reciprocal depression, evolves
**Early repolarisation** | concave, notched or slurred J point, stable
**Pericarditis** | concave, widespread, **PR depression**
**LBBB** | discordant: ST opposite the QRS}}

[[Convex, in one territory, with reciprocal depression is STEMI. Concave with a notched J point in a well young man is early repolarisation. Concave, widespread, with PR depression is pericarditis.]]

A caution about the word concave, because it becomes a trap. An infarct in its first minutes can still be concave. So a concave shape does not exclude an occlusion. Territory and the mirror decide. If the opposite cameras show reciprocal depression, treat it as an infarct whatever the curve looks like.

Now the grand test question. An athlete of twenty-nine with no symptoms. J point elevation of zero point one five millivolts, which is one and a half millimetres, from V3 to V5. Concave, with no reciprocal change. That is early repolarisation. The tempting options are myocarditis and Brugada. Myocarditis brings symptoms and a troponin rise. Brugada is a coved, downsloping elevation confined to V1 and V2. An athlete without symptoms, with concave elevation and nothing in the mirror, has a normal heart.

That closes the section on the blocked artery. You know why the ST segment moves, how much counts, whose territory it is, and where an infarct hides. The next section turns the question round. If the ST segment only reports a difference in voltage between neighbours, what else, apart from a closed artery, can create one?
lesson.cap: STEMI: convex, territorial, reciprocal. Early repolarisation: notched J, concave. Pericarditis: diffuse concave + PR depression. Aneurysm: ST elevation persisting over Q waves.

spine: Injured muscle cannot hold its resting potential or plateau: an injury current flows and the ST segment shifts towards the injured zone.
Full-thickness injury: ST elevation in the facing leads, reciprocal depression opposite. Inner-layer injury: ST depression that does not localise, aVR up.
Sequence: hyperacute T, ST elevation, Q waves (permanent), T inversion, ST settles by about 2 weeks. Measure at the J point: 1 mm; V2–V3 2.5 / 2.0 / 1.5 mm.
II, III, aVF = RCA (III > II, aVL down) or LCx; I, aVL, V5–V6 = LCx or diagonal; V1–V4 = LAD; V1 elevation + new RBBB = proximal LAD.
Hidden: posterior (V1–V3 ST depression, tall R; V7–V9 ≥0.5 mm), RV (V4R ≥1 mm: fluid, no nitrates), left main (≥6 leads down, aVR up).
Wellens = pain-free, reopened LAD (T inversion V2–V3): early angiography, no stress test. de Winter = painful, occluded LAD: immediate PCI.

questions.text: ST and T changes that are not a blocked artery: pericardium, lungs, brain and the scar

open.text:
The ST segment knows nothing about arteries. It reports one thing only: whether neighbouring patches of muscle are sitting at the same voltage. A closed artery is the commonest reason for them to differ. It is not the only one.

So ST elevation and coronary occlusion are not the same statement. An inflamed pericardium, a right ventricle stretched by a clot in the lung, a surge of catecholamines from an injured brain, an old scar that bulges: each of them can shift the ST segment or flip the T wave, with every coronary artery wide open.

This section is a set of impostors, and of each you'll ask three questions. Does the change follow one artery's territory? Is there a mirror image in the opposite cameras? Does it evolve over hours? An infarct answers yes three times. Each impostor fails at least one.

Listen for three traps. Clot-dissolving drugs given to pericarditis or a brain bleed. The famous sign of pulmonary embolism that is present in only a minority. And a syndrome said never to raise the ST segment, which in fact does it often.

Begin with the inflamed sac.

steps.bridge: Pericarditis is concave and widespread. Two other diagnoses lift the ST segment in the same concave way.

lesson.text:
Here is a puzzle. The pericardium is a sheet of fibrous tissue. It has no action potential and makes no electricity. So how can inflaming it change the ECG?

It can't, on its own. What changes the ECG is the thin outer skin of heart muscle lying directly under the inflamed sac. Inflammation spreads into it, those cells can no longer hold their voltage, and you have an injury current again. The difference from an infarct is the shape of the injured zone. An infarct injures one wall, through its full thickness, in one artery's territory. Pericarditis injures a shallow layer over the whole surface of the heart.

Now use the cameras. The injured layer is on the outside, facing every camera on the chest and limbs, so they all record ST elevation at once: limb leads and chest leads together, fitting no single artery. The muscle underneath is alive, so the segment keeps its natural concave curve and no Q wave ever forms. And where is the mirror? The only camera standing opposite the whole surface is the one that looks into the cavity from the right shoulder. So aVR, and often V1, show ST depression. Outside those two leads there is no reciprocal change.

The second sign is the one that names the diagnosis. The atria are wrapped in the same sac. Their outer layer is injured too, and an atrial injury current shifts the segment that follows the P wave: the PR segment. It is pushed down in most leads, and lifted in aVR, the mirror again. This is why the baseline matters. In pericarditis, measure the ST segment against the TP segment, because the PR segment has moved.

[[Pericarditis: widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression, in limb and chest leads together. aVR shows the mirror image, ST depression with PR elevation. No Q waves, no reciprocal depression elsewhere.]]

Then the time course, which is slow, and its order is itself a test. Stage one, over the first hours to days, is the ST elevation with PR depression. In stage two the ST segment returns to the baseline. Only then, in stage three, do the T waves invert. In stage four, weeks later, everything is normal again. Compare the infarct, where the T wave inverts while the ST segment is still raised. So ST elevation and T inversion together, in the same leads, point away from pericarditis and towards ischaemia.

{{**Pericarditis, four stages**
1 | diffuse concave ST elevation + PR depression (aVR: opposite)
2 | ST returns to baseline
3 | T waves invert
4 | normal
Classic changes in up to **60%** only; sinus tachycardia common}}

Two last facts. Sinus tachycardia is common, from pain and fever. And the classic picture appears in only up to sixty per cent of cases, so a normal tracing does not exclude pericarditis. The wrong option reads: no ST elevation, so not pericarditis.

What you do about it, the diagnostic criteria and the drugs, belongs to the pericardium packet. Here, stay with the tracing, because this patient is sitting in the chest pain room and two other diagnoses lift the ST segment in the same concave way.
lesson.cap: Pericarditis: 1 diffuse ST elevation + PR depression (aVR opposite), 2 ST settles, 3 T inverts, 4 normal. Classic changes in only about 60%.

lesson.text:
Concave ST elevation has three common owners: pericarditis, early repolarisation, and the first minutes of an infarct. Separate them one pair at a time.

First, pericarditis against early repolarisation. You know where early repolarisation comes from: the notch at the start of the plateau, more marked in the outer layer, drawing a small hook at the J point in a healthy young man. Nothing is inflamed. So the differences follow. Early repolarisation lives mainly in the chest leads; pericarditis spreads to the limb leads as well. Early repolarisation leaves the PR segment alone; pericarditis depresses it. Early repolarisation has the fish-hook J point in V4 and tall, prominent T waves. And it is the same next week and next year, while pericarditis moves through its stages.

When the two still look alike, there is one measurement, in V6. Take the height of the ST elevation and divide it by the height of the T wave. Early repolarisation has a small ST step under a tall T wave, so the ratio is low. In pericarditis the ST segment is raised out of proportion to the T wave. The cut is one quarter.

[[In V6, ST elevation more than a quarter of the height of the T wave favours pericarditis. Less than a quarter favours early repolarisation.]]

{{**In V6: ST height ÷ T height**
Early repolarisation | **< 0.25**
Acute pericarditis | **> 0.25**
Early repolarisation: chest leads, no PR depression, fish-hook J point in V4, tall T, young men, no treatment}}

Early repolarisation is seen in young men, and it needs no treatment. The exam version is the athlete without symptoms, and the wrong options are myocarditis and pericarditis, both of which need a patient who is unwell.

Second, pericarditis against the infarct. This is the pair where a mistake does harm in either direction. Give a clot-dissolving drug to pericarditis and you can bleed into the sac. Miss an occlusion and muscle dies. Everything that separates them is the one difference you've already built: an infarct follows an artery, and pericarditis follows the whole surface.

So in pericarditis the elevation is diffuse; in an infarct it stays inside one territory. Pericarditis depresses the PR segment; an infarct does not. Pericarditis changes over days and weeks and never forms a Q wave; an infarct changes over hours and does. In the inferior leads there is a fine point from the angles: an inferior infarct from the right coronary raises lead three more than lead two, while pericarditis, whose shift points towards the apex, raises lead two more than lead three.

But one feature outweighs the rest, and it is the mirror. An infarct has cameras facing away from it, and they show reciprocal depression: aVL in an inferior infarct, the inferior leads in a high lateral one. Pericarditis has no opposite camera except aVR.

[[Reciprocal ST depression in any lead other than aVR and V1 means infarction until proved otherwise. It is the best single feature separating a STEMI from pericarditis.]]

NEET's trap is to rely on shape. Concave ST elevation does not exclude a STEMI, as you heard. Territory and reciprocal change decide.

Your card for this pair has one more row, electrical alternans. You met it when the cameras lost the signal: the heart swinging in a large effusion. It means the sac has filled, and it belongs to tamponade.

So far each impostor was a living heart. The next is a dead patch of one.
lesson.cap: V6 ST/T ratio: ≥ 0.25 favours pericarditis, < 0.25 early repolarisation. PR depression and diffuse spread also favour pericarditis.

lesson.text:
Go back to the last stage of the infarct. The ST segment settles within about two weeks, and the Q wave stays. Sometimes the ST segment never settles. Weeks later it is still raised over deep Q waves. What has happened?

A large infarct through the full thickness of the wall, not reopened in time, heals as a thin sheet of scar. With every beat, while the living muscle contracts, that sheet bulges outward. This is a left ventricular aneurysm. It follows fewer than five in a hundred infarcts, fewer still since primary PCI, and it sits where the big anterior infarcts are: the anteroseptal wall and the apex. So the persisting elevation is usually in the front chest leads. Exactly why a scar keeps the ST segment up is debated. The likeliest source is the living muscle at its rim, stretched with every beat. You don't need the mechanism. You need the pattern.

[[ST elevation that persists more than two weeks after an infarct, over Q waves, with no new pain and no new rise in troponin, is a left ventricular aneurysm, not a new infarct.]]

NEET's wrong option is re-infarction and a second trip for reperfusion. Run the three questions and you won't take it. Does it evolve over hours? No, it is the same on every tracing. Is there a mirror image? No. And the old ECG, if you can find it, shows the same thing.

That gives you a three-way reading, and you've now built every part of it. Q waves with a flat ST segment: an old, healed infarct. ST elevation with symptoms or a rising troponin: an acute one. Q waves with ST elevation that has been there for weeks: an aneurysm.

The rest of the card is the aneurysm's consequences. Blood stagnates in the pouch, a clot forms at the apex and can travel. How long to anticoagulate, and when a surgeon is needed, is taught with the complications of infarction in the second ACS packet.

Now leave the left ventricle altogether. The next impostor draws its changes in the front chest leads, and the problem is in the lungs.

lesson.text:
A clot lodges in the pulmonary artery. Nothing has happened to a coronary artery, and yet the ECG changes. Why?

Because the right ventricle has just been handed a load it wasn't built for. You'll recall it is a thin-walled pump made for low pressure. Suddenly it must push against a blocked outflow. It stretches, its wall tension soars, and its inner layer becomes short of blood. This is called right ventricular strain. Every ECG sign of pulmonary embolism is that strained ventricle, seen by the cameras that sit over it.

Take them in order of how often they appear. The commonest finding is plain sinus tachycardia. Next comes T wave inversion in V1 to V4, the chest leads that lie over the right ventricle, often with inversion in lead three and aVF as well. That is the ischaemic, strained right ventricle repolarising late, just as you learned for the left. Then the stretched ventricle delays its own wiring. The right bundle branch runs just under its inner surface, so a new right bundle branch block appears, complete or incomplete. The axis swings to the right, towards the overloaded chamber. The right atrium, stretched behind it, may add a tall peaked P wave or tip into atrial fibrillation.

And then the famous one. S1 Q3 T3: a deep S wave in lead one, with a Q wave and an inverted T wave in lead three. It is the same rightward swing, seen in two limb leads. But it is present in only one or two patients in ten, and it appears in other causes of sudden right heart strain too. NEET's trap is to offer it as the commonest or the diagnostic sign. It is neither. Nor does a normal ECG exclude an embolus.

[[Pulmonary embolism on the ECG is right ventricular strain. Sinus tachycardia is commonest, then T inversion in V1 to V4. S1 Q3 T3 is seen in a minority and is not diagnostic.]]

Now two confusions to settle.

First, strain against infarction of the right ventricle. They are different pictures. Infarction is ST elevation, in the right-sided lead V4R, riding on an inferior infarct. Strain is T wave inversion, in the front chest leads, with S1 Q3 T3. One is a closed right coronary. The other is a blocked pulmonary artery.

Second, and this is the mimic that matters here: T inversion across the front chest leads is also Wellens. How do you tell a clot in the lung from a critical LAD? Look at where the inversion is deepest and what else is inverted. In pulmonary embolism it is deepest in V1 and V2, and lead three is inverted as well. In Wellens it is deepest in V2 and V3, and the inferior leads are spared. T inversion in both V1 and lead three, in a breathless patient with a fast pulse, is an embolus until proved otherwise.

Last, a score you skipped in the September paper. The Daniel score grades how much strain the ECG shows, out of twenty-one points. You need only the big items.

{{**Daniel ECG score (max 21)**
Heart rate > 100 | **2**
Incomplete RBBB | **2**
Complete RBBB | **3**
T inversion in all of V1–V4 | **4**
Complete S1Q3T3 | **2**
Score **≥ 10**: severe pulmonary hypertension (systolic PA pressure > 50 mmHg)}}

A heart rate above one hundred scores two. Incomplete right bundle branch block scores two, complete scores three. T inversion in all of V1 to V4 scores four. A complete S1 Q3 T3 scores two. The remaining points come from grading how deep the T inversion is in each lead. The stem gave a heart rate of one hundred and eighteen, incomplete right bundle branch block and T inversion from V1 to V4. Two, two and four: eight, and eight was the keyed answer. Know the catch, though. In the full score an inverted T wave in V2 and in V3 adds at least one more point each, even when it is shallow. So if a stem gives the depth of the T waves, add those points. If it gives none, count the three big items as the examiner did. A total of ten or more points to severe pulmonary hypertension, a systolic pulmonary artery pressure above fifty millimetres of mercury. It is very specific and not at all sensitive, so a low score reassures nobody.

How the embolus is risk-classed and treated belongs to the right heart packet. One more organ can write on the front chest leads, and it isn't in the chest at all.
lesson.cap: PE: sinus tachycardia commonest; T inversion V1–V4 (RV strain); RBBB; right axis. S1Q3T3 is uncommon and non-specific.

lesson.text:
An aneurysm bursts at the base of the brain. Within hours the ECG is abnormal in the great majority of these patients, and there is nothing wrong with their coronary arteries. This is the brain writing on the heart.

The route is the sympathetic system, and you know its hand on the wiring. A sudden rise in pressure inside the skull, or blood around the hypothalamus, releases a storm of catecholamines. Not only from the adrenal glands into the blood, but straight out of the sympathetic nerve endings inside the heart muscle. The cells are flooded with calcium. Repolarisation becomes slow and uneven, and some cells are stunned or killed outright.

Now read that on the ECG. Slow, uneven repolarisation is phase three, so it shows in the T wave and the QT interval. The classic picture is the cerebral T wave: deep, wide, symmetric inversion across the chest leads, far broader than an ischaemic T wave, sitting on a long QT interval. Prominent U waves may follow. The ST segment may be raised or depressed. And because a long QT invites early beats to fall on the T wave, there are arrhythmias, up to torsades de pointes. That is why you correct potassium and magnesium early in these patients, both of which run low after a subarachnoid bleed.

[[After a subarachnoid haemorrhage, deep wide T inversion with a long QT is the cerebral T wave. It comes from a catecholamine surge, not from a blocked coronary artery.]]

When the surge is severe the muscle itself is stunned. This is neurogenic stunned myocardium, the most serious cardiac complication on your card. The troponin rises, in about one patient in five. The echo shows segments that have stopped moving. And those segments do not match the territory of any one coronary artery, because nerve endings, not an artery, did the damage. It recovers over days to weeks. The same surge, acting on the lung vessels, gives neurogenic pulmonary oedema.

{{**Subarachnoid haemorrhage and the heart**
ECG abnormal in most
Cerebral T waves: deep, wide, inverted; **long QT**; U waves; ST up or down
Troponin rise about 20%
Stunned myocardium: wall motion loss fits **no coronary territory**, reversible
Correct K and Mg: torsades risk}}

NEET's trap here is the dangerous one. Sudden severe headache, a collapse, then ST change and a raised troponin, and the option reads: acute coronary syndrome, give antiplatelets and heparin, or thrombolyse. In a patient with a fresh bleed in the head that is a catastrophe. The story decides. A thunderclap headache or a fall in consciousness before the ECG changes means the brain comes first, and the scan comes before any drug that affects clotting.

Apply the three questions and the impostor is exposed. Territory? No, the changes are widespread. Mirror image? No. And the T waves are too wide and the QT too long for ordinary ischaemia. That also separates it from Wellens, where the QT is close to normal and the patient gives a history of angina.

One more sign from the same patient, in the opposite direction. When pressure inside the skull rises far enough to squeeze the brainstem, blood pressure climbs and the heart slows. That is the Cushing reflex. So sinus bradycardia with hypertension in a patient with a head injury is the brain again, working through the vagus.

The rest of that card, the sodium and the glucose, belongs to the neurology packets.

Now take the same catecholamine surge and remove the head injury. It has a name of its own.
lesson.cap: SAH or raised ICP: giant, wide inverted T waves and a long QT, often with troponin rise — neurogenic, not coronary.
